patients.summary: Thirty-something high school shop teacher who also stocks part time at a medical-supply warehouse, with childhood-onset mild persistent asthma managed on albuterol alone. documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT / ESTABLISH CARE

31M here to set up with us. Was at another primary care office for years, drifted away from it. No acute concerns today.

Asthma since he was a kid, probably around age 6 or 7. Only ever used a rescue inhaler. Uses albuterol a few times a week, mostly when he exercises or when it's cold out. No ED visits or steroid bursts he can recall as an adult. No nighttime symptoms currently.

PMH: asthma as above. No surgeries.
Meds: albuterol HFA 90 mcg, 2 puffs q4-6h prn.
Allergies: no drug allergies. Environmental: dust mites, seasonal pollen.
FH: mother has asthma. Father has hay fever and high blood pressure.
SH: teaches shop at the high school. Also works part time stocking at a medical-supply warehouse on weekends and some evenings. Never smoked. Drinks socially, 1-2 a week. Single, lives in Northampton.

ROS: negative except as above.

Exam: Well appearing, comfortable. HEENT unremarkable, TMs clear, oropharynx clear. Neck supple, no adenopathy. Lungs clear bilaterally, good air movement, no wheeze. Heart RRR, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities without edema. Skin no rash.

PHQ-2: 0.

A/P
1. Mild persistent asthma, childhood onset. Using albuterol a few times a week with exertion/cold. Lungs clear today. Continue albuterol as needed. Reviewed technique with him, he's fine.
2. Health maintenance: CBC, CMP, lipids. One-time HIV and hep C screening, he agreed. Requested prior records for vaccine history. Flu shot this fall.

RTC 1 year or sooner prn.

reports.text:
PULMONARY FUNCTION LABORATORY
Test date: 04/12/2023
Referring: primary care
Indication: asthma evaluation
Patient: 34-year-old male, never smoker. Height 180.3 cm. Albuterol withheld morning of test.

Spirometry, pre and post bronchodilator (albuterol 4 puffs via spacer):
- FVC: pre 5.18 L (98% predicted); post 5.30 L
- FEV1: pre 3.52 L (82% predicted); post 4.02 L, change +500 mL (+14%)
- FEV1/FVC: pre 0.68; post 0.76

Technique: good effort, three acceptable and repeatable maneuvers. Flow-volume loops show concave expiratory limb before bronchodilator, improved after.
reports.conclusion: Airflow obstruction with a significant response to bronchodilator, consistent with reversible obstruction. FVC normal.

documents.title: Pulmonology Follow-up
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE PULMONOLOGY GROUP
Date of service: 10/13/2023
Re: Chad Bradley, DOB 12/29/1988

Dear Doctor,

I saw Mr. Bradley, a 34-year-old man, today to follow up his April spirometry and his asthma. He has had asthma since childhood and has relied only on an albuterol inhaler, which until recently he needed a few times a week, mainly with exercise and in cold air. For roughly the last two months he has been reaching for it nearly every day, and one or two nights a week he wakes up coughing and wheezy. No recent respiratory infections and no hospital stays. He told me he has not seen a clinician in more than a year.

Medications: albuterol HFA 90 mcg, 2 puffs every 4-6 hours as needed.
Allergies: dust mites, seasonal pollen. No drug allergies.
Family history: asthma in his mother; allergic rhinitis and hypertension in his father.
Social: teaches high school shop; also works part time stocking at a warehouse, where he is regularly around dust and fumes. Never smoker.

Exam: BMI 24. Comfortable, speaking in full sentences. There is mild expiratory wheezing on auscultation. Remainder of the exam, including HEENT, cardiac, and extremities, is normal.

Studies: peak expiratory flow today is 80% of his predicted value. Spirometry in our lab in April showed reversible airflow obstruction.

Assessment: Asthma with recent loss of control. He is not having an acute exacerbation and can be managed as an outpatient, but his current pattern of symptoms tells us the severity of his asthma has changed. Workplace exposure to dust and fumes is noted.

Plan: continue albuterol as needed. Limit exposure to dust and fumes at the warehouse where he can. We are glad to see him again whenever needed.

Thank you for allowing us to participate in his care.

Pulmonology

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
COMMUNITY HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Visit date: 03/27/2025
Patient: Chad Bradley, 36M

CC: fever, aches, headache, cough

HPI: 36 y/o man with asthma since childhood (seen by pulmonology in Oct 2023 for worsening control) who came on abruptly two days ago with fever, diffuse muscle aches, headache, and a dry cough. Feels "run down." Highest temp at home 38.2 C (100.8 F). He teaches high school and says a number of his students have been out sick with the same thing. Flu is going around and we are still in the thick of the season.

PMH: asthma. PSH: none.
Meds: albuterol HFA 90 mcg 2 puffs q4-6h prn.
Allergies: dust mites, seasonal pollen. NKDA.
FH: mother asthma; father allergic rhinitis, HTN.
SH: never smoker; 1-2 drinks/week; HS shop teacher and part-time warehouse stocker.

Triage vitals: T 38.3 C (100.9 F), BP 120/78, HR 88, RR 16.

Exam: Tired appearing but nontoxic. Pharynx mildly red, no exudate. No cervical adenopathy. Lungs clear, no wheezes, no increased work of breathing. Heart regular. Abdomen soft. Skin without rash. Neuro nonfocal.

ED course: rapid influenza A+B antigen positive for influenza A, negative for B.

MDM: Influenza A, within 48 hours of onset, in a patient with asthma. Lungs clear, oxygenating well, no signs of pneumonia or asthma flare. Will treat with oseltamivir. Supportive care.

Disposition: discharged home.
Dx: Influenza A.
Rx: oseltamivir 75 mg PO BID x 5 days.
Instructions: fluids, rest, acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever and aches, albuterol as needed. Stay home until fever-free 24 hours without medicine. Return for difficulty breathing, wheezing not relieved by inhaler, chest pain, or confusion. Follow up with PCP.

documents.title: Flu
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Went to the ER yesterday afternoon, I have the flu (A). They gave me Tamiflu. School needs a note for being out through at least Monday. Can you do that or does it have to come from the ER?

documents.title: RE: Flu
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Sorry you're sick. I have the ER record. Work note is attached, out through Monday 3/31, back Tuesday if you've been fever free for a day. Finish all 10 doses of the Tamiflu. Use your albuterol if you get wheezy. If your breathing gets worse or the inhaler isn't helping, call us right away, any hour. Our nurse will check on you Monday.

documents.title: Post-ED Check-in
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt for f/u after ED visit for influenza A. Fever gone since Saturday. Still has a dry cough and is tired. Used albuterol maybe twice a day over the weekend, a bit more than his usual, now tapering off. No SOB at rest, no chest pain. Last Tamiflu dose tomorrow morning. Plans to return to work tomorrow. Telehealth with PCP set for 4/8. Reviewed return precautions.

documents.title: Occupational Health Visit
documents.author: occupational medicine
documents.body:
OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH SERVICES
Date of service: 10/06/2025
Employee: Chad Bradley, DOB 12/29/1988, age 36
Employer: medical-supply distribution warehouse (part-time stocker)
Visit type: mandatory education, at employer request

Reason: Over a 10-day stretch at the start of this flu season, several warehouse staff came down with influenza. The employer is requiring each employee to complete an infection-prevention session with us.

Health history (employee report): asthma since childhood, uses albuterol HFA 90 mcg as needed. Had influenza in March of this year. Allergies: dust mites and seasonal pollen. Family history of asthma in his mother, and of allergic rhinitis and high blood pressure in his father. Never smoker; drinks socially 1-2 times a week. Also works full time as a high school shop teacher.

Education provided: respiratory hygiene during flu season. Cover every cough or sneeze with a tissue and discard it; when no tissue is at hand, cough or sneeze into the upper sleeve or bend of the elbow rather than the hands. Turn away from coworkers and from product, including packaged sterile supplies. Clean hands before going back to handling stock. Do not come to work with fever or flu-like symptoms; report illness to the supervisor. Employee verbalized understanding and completed the session.

No restrictions. Cleared to continue regular duty.

Occupational Medicine

PHQ-2: 0.

Plan:
- Asthma: continue albuterol as needed.
- Vaccines current: flu and Covid 10/16, Tdap and PCV20 2024.
- CBC, CMP today.
- Next physical in a year.
